安塔拉排笛主要用於「西庫里」音樂，見於安第斯、秘魯、玻利維亞，尤其的的喀喀湖周邊: The antara is used mainly in "sikuri" music, found in the Andes, in Peru and Bolivia, especially in the Aymara-speaking area around Lake Titicaca. Traditionally two players each hold one of the two rows of pipes and blow alternately, which produces the stereo effect of Andean music, and rural ensembles still keep this arrangement; today there is also solo playing, and the instrument has been standardised to fit Western music.
安塔拉排笛屬氣鳴樂器，發聲依靠氣流進入管腔。來源未載具體持琴姿勢，可依其結構操作: The antara is an aerophone; it sounds when a stream of air enters the tubes. The source does not record a specific playing position, so it can be worked out from the structure: the instrument is divided into two rows of pipes, and the player must blow the two rows alternately in the order of the scale to produce a complete one. Traditionally two players each hold one complementary row, and today one player blowing both rows is also common. A beginner can first practise the notes and the order of alternation on each row separately, then play with another player so that the notes follow one another into a melody.
安塔拉排笛為氣鳴樂器，發聲體主要為竹管或蘆葦管。傳統安塔拉多用生長於安第斯山林帶: The antara is an aerophone, and its sound-producing body is mainly bamboo or cane tubes. The traditional antara is usually made of cane that grows in the Andean forest belt, with the pipes bound into a trapezoid by one or two strips of cane. Other siku are also often of bamboo, and some are made from condor feathers, bone and similar materials. The kind of bamboo affects the timbre: thin-walled bamboo is louder and more resonant but breaks easily. Some variants add open auxiliary tubes at the front to change the timbre, and the rectangular siku has plugs inside the tubes to adjust the resonating length. The materials of the other parts are not stated in the source.
安塔拉排笛（Antara）在來源中僅被標記為安地斯傳統排笛，亦稱西庫（Siku）: In the source the antara is marked only as a traditional Andean panpipe, also called siku, and as an aerophone. The source does not record its specific construction, its way of playing, the people who use it or the occasions for it, and it gives no Hornbostel–Sachs number; it therefore cannot be assumed to be a reed instrument, or to belong to Iran, Azerbaijan or the Caucasus. What can be confirmed from the source is that it is another name for, or a variant of, a panpipe, and that it is classified by how it sounds as an aerophone.
安塔拉排笛（Siku）傳統上源自秘魯與玻利維亞的艾馬拉人，分布於安第斯山區，尤其: The antara (siku) comes traditionally from the Aymara of Peru and Bolivia and is distributed through the Andes, especially around Lake Titicaca. Because the mountain geography is so broken, each community developed its own tuning, shape, size and style of playing. In earlier times women often held two smaller panpipes and blew alternately with others to complete the scale, a fixed pairing within religious and community life; the instrument was also used to attract wild goats. Today it has been standardised to be compatible with Western music, and playing by one person on both rows has become more common than two players each holding a row, but rural ensembles keep the tradition.
